patient.name: Tomasz Nowak
patient.complaint: Searing pain every time he opens his bowels, with bright red blood on the paper
background: Taking co-codamol for a back injury for the last 2 months
Hard, infrequent stools since starting it
No weight loss, no diarrhoea, no family history of bowel cancer

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with severe pain on defecation and bright red blood on the stool or paper: the pain separates it from haemorrhoids, and an off-midline fissure is a red flag.

points: Tomasz, 34, dreads the toilet: pain like **passing glass**.
Bright red blood on the paper and streaking the stool.
Pain lingers for an hour afterwards; he now holds stool in.
Hard stools since starting **co-codamol** 2 months ago.

steps.lead: Hard stools from codeine have torn Tomasz's **anoderm**. Fissures sit at the **posterior midline** in most patients.

visual.title: Tomasz's pain on defecation
visual.label: Tomasz 9/10
visual.caption: Severe pain with defecation is the fissure hallmark; haemorrhoids usually bleed painlessly.

steps.lead: Pain on defecation, bright red bleeding, **fear of opening his bowels** and anal spasm: Tomasz's history is classic.

steps.q: What single feature best separates Tomasz's problem from internal haemorrhoids?
steps.r: Both bleed bright red and both follow constipation. **Pain** is the fissure; internal haemorrhoids are typically **painless**.

steps.lead: Tomasz's **severe pain** is the giveaway: fissures hurt, haemorrhoids bleed painlessly.

points: Gentle buttock parting (no PR: too painful).
A small **sentinel skin tag** at its outer end.

steps.lead: The **sentinel tag** tells you Tomasz's fissure has been there a while: it is becoming **chronic** and non-healing.

steps.title: Painful or painless? Anal causes of bright red bleeding
head: Feature
Anal fissure
Internal haemorrhoids
Thrombosed external haemorrhoid
Perianal abscess

steps.lead: Tomasz's tear is **midline**. If it were off to the side, think **Crohn's**, anal cancer or an STI.

steps.text: Do not attempt a digital rectal exam on Tomasz to 'confirm' a typical fissure. It is too painful, and the diagnosis is made by **inspection**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where a typical fissure needs none (clinical diagnosis), while an off-midline fissure needs faecal calprotectin, gastroenterology or a 2-week-wait referral.

steps.q: Tomasz has a typical posterior midline fissure. Which investigation does he need?
steps.r: A typical fissure in a young man with no red flags is a **clinical diagnosis**; no tests needed.

steps.lead: Tomasz's history and the visible midline tear are enough: **anal fissure is diagnosed clinically**.

steps.title: Is this fissure typical?
nodes: Posterior (or anterior) midline, clear cause → treat
Off-midline or multiple → look for a cause
Diarrhoea, weight loss, mouth ulcers → calprotectin, gastroenterology

steps.title: If Tomasz's fissure had been lateral, with diarrhoea
steps.text: A raised calprotectin points to inflammatory bowel disease such as **Crohn's**.

steps.lead: A **lateral** fissure would need calprotectin and gastroenterology; a suspicious one goes on the **2-week-wait** pathway.

visual.title: Faecal calprotectin
visual.label: Lateral-fissure example
visual.caption: Tomasz's midline fissure needs no calprotectin; this shows when it would.

steps.text: Midline + clear cause (constipation) = treat. **Off-midline** = investigate. That one fact earns most fissure investigation marks.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (fibre, fluids, laxatives, analgesia) or 'next step' in a chronic fissure (0.2% GTN, then diltiazem, then botulinum toxin or sphincterotomy).

steps.q: When Tomasz first saw the GP, 3 days in, what was the right plan?
steps.r: An **acute** fissure is treated conservatively: soften the stool and treat pain. **Avoid topical steroids**.

steps.lead: Tomasz is told to stop codeine if he can, take **ispaghula husk**, drink more, use paracetamol and a lubricant or topical anaesthetic before defecation.

points: Eight weeks later, still painful despite softer stools.
The tear has not healed; the **sentinel tag** is bigger.

steps.lead: Tomasz starts **0.2% GTN ointment** for 6 to 8 weeks. Two weeks in, he stops it because of **headaches**, so he switches to **topical diltiazem**.

visual.title: Tomasz's pain score on treatment
visual.caption: Diltiazem relaxes the sphincter without GTN's headaches; the fissure heals by week 8.

steps.title: Anal fissure treatment ladder
nodes: Acute: fibre, fluids, laxatives, analgesia, lubricant; no steroids
GTN not tolerated or fails: topical diltiazem or oral nifedipine

steps.lead: Had Tomasz's fissure failed both drugs, **botulinum toxin** or **lateral internal sphincterotomy** would be next.
If Tomasz could not pass stool at all or had unbearable pain, he would need **urgent surgical review**.

steps.text: Topical **steroid** creams are for haemorrhoids, not fissures. Do not pick them as fissure treatment.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the posterior midline heals poorly (watershed blood supply plus sphincter spasm), and how GTN and calcium channel blockers work.

steps.lead: Tomasz's hard stool tore the anoderm where blood supply is poorest, the **posterior midline watershed**, and his tight internal sphincter stopped it healing.

steps.title: The fissure vicious cycle
nodes: Pain triggers internal anal sphincter spasm
Less blood flow to the posterior midline
Poor healing, more pain, more spasm

steps.lead: Each time Tomasz strained, the pain made his sphincter clamp down, reducing blood flow further: a **cycle** of pain, spasm and poor healing.

steps.q: How does GTN help Tomasz's fissure heal?
o: Releases nitric oxide to relax the internal sphincter
steps.r: GTN is a **nitric oxide donor**: it relaxes the smooth muscle of the internal sphincter, improving blood flow.

steps.lead: Diltiazem worked for Tomasz the same way: **relaxing the internal sphincter** and restoring blood flow. Botox and sphincterotomy do it chemically or surgically.

visual.title: What treatment changes
visual.caption: Lower tone, more blood flow: the cycle breaks and the fissure heals.

steps.lead: Tomasz's tear is in the **expected place** for a mechanical fissure. An off-midline tear does not follow this pattern, so look for disease.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has 5 days of severe anal pain when she opens her bowels, lasting an hour afterwards. There is bright red blood on the toilet paper. She has been constipated since starting iron tablets. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. There is no anal lump.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: anal pain plus bleeding. Decide painful or painless, and constant or with defecation.

clues: severe anal pain when she opens her bowels
bright red blood on the toilet paper
steps.x: Pain **with defecation**, bright red blood on paper, constipation trigger, no lump.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anal fissure**.

elim: A fistula gives discharge and recurrent abscesses, not defecation pain with fresh blood.
Internal haemorrhoids bleed **painlessly**.
An abscess causes constant throbbing pain, a tender swelling and often fever.
A thrombosed haemorrhoid is a tender purple lump with constant pain; there is no lump.

steps.x: **A. Anal fissure.** Rule: painful bleeding with defecation = fissure; painless = haemorrhoids.

technique.stem: A 22 year old man has 6 weeks of anal pain and bleeding. Examination shows a fissure at the lateral (3 o'clock) position. He also has 2 months of loose stools, mouth ulcers and 4 kg weight loss. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: An investigation question with an atypical fissure.
**Off-midline** fissure + diarrhoea + mouth ulcers + weight loss = possible **Crohn's**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Faecal calprotectin**, then gastroenterology referral.

elim: HSV gives painful vesicles and ulcers, and does not explain diarrhoea and weight loss.
Endoanal ultrasound is for sphincter injury or fistula anatomy.
An off-midline fissure is a red flag; it must be investigated.
CA-125 is an ovarian marker.

steps.x: **C. Faecal calprotectin.** Rule: lateral fissure = look for Crohn's, cancer or STI.

technique.stem: A 41 year old man has had a posterior midline anal fissure for 5 months. He has used fibre, laxatives and topical 0.2% GTN for 8 weeks, then topical diltiazem for 8 weeks, without healing. He is in severe pain.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: 'Next step' after medical treatment has failed.
Chronic, **refractory** fissure after GTN and a calcium channel blocker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Surgery to reduce sphincter tone: **lateral internal sphincterotomy** (or botulinum toxin).

elim: Haemorrhoidal artery ligation treats haemorrhoids.
Systemic steroids have no role.
Banding is for internal haemorrhoids.
Topical steroids are avoided in fissures.

steps.x: **B. Lateral internal sphincterotomy.**

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman with a chronic anal fissure is prescribed topical glyceryl trinitrate ointment. After a week she has headaches but less pain on defecation.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which this treatment promotes healing?
o: Relaxation of the internal anal sphincter

steps.x: A drug mechanism question in anal fissure.
GTN is a **nitric oxide** donor (hence vasodilator headaches).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: NO **relaxes the internal anal sphincter** and increases blood flow, breaking the spasm cycle.

elim: GTN is not antibacterial.
That is a local anaesthetic.
That is an osmotic laxative.
GTN does not act on growth factors.

steps.x: **D. Relaxation of the internal anal sphincter.**

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has 1 week of tearing anal pain on defecation and bright red blood on the stool surface. He has been constipated. He is afraid to open his bowels. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. There is no perianal swelling.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Severe pain on defecation with fresh blood after constipation, and fear of opening the bowels, is anal fissure; haemorrhoids are painless.

steps.x: Diagnosis of painful rectal bleeding.

clues: bright red blood on the stool surface
steps.x: Pain with defecation, fresh blood, constipation, fear of defecation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anal fissure**.

elim: Fistula causes discharge and recurrent abscesses.
Internal haemorrhoids are painless.
No swelling or fever.
Pilonidal sinus is in the natal cleft, not related to defecation.

steps.x: **A. Anal fissure.**

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has 2 weeks of severe pain on opening her bowels and blood on the toilet paper after constipation. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Gentle parting of the buttocks is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Linear tear in the posterior midline
practice.e: A typical fissure is a linear tear in the anoderm at the posterior midline.

steps.x: 'Most likely finding' in a typical fissure.

clues: severe pain on opening her bowels
steps.x: Classic fissure history with a mechanical cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **linear tear at the posterior midline**.

elim: That is a perianal abscess.
Multiple lateral ulcers suggest Crohn's, HSV or syphilis.
That is a thrombosed external haemorrhoid.
That is a fistula opening.

steps.x: **B. Posterior midline tear.**

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has had pain on defecation and occasional bright red bleeding for 4 months. Softer stools have helped only a little. Examination shows a posterior midline tear with exposed muscle fibres and a skin tag at its outer edge.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A non-healing posterior midline fissure lasting months with a sentinel skin tag is a chronic anal fissure.

steps.x: Diagnosis: decide acute versus chronic.

clues: skin tag at its outer edge
steps.x: Long duration, non-healing, **sentinel tag**, exposed sphincter fibres.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic anal fissure**.

elim: Months of symptoms and a sentinel tag are not acute.
Cancer is off-midline, hard and irregular, often with weight loss.
A fistula has an external opening with discharge.
The tag is a sentinel pile, not a prolapsed haemorrhoid.

steps.x: **C. Chronic anal fissure.**

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has a painful anal fissure at the lateral position. She also has 3 months of loose stools, crampy abdominal pain and weight loss. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of the fissure?
practice.e: An off-midline fissure with diarrhoea, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers suggests Crohn's disease, a recognised fissure risk factor.

steps.x: Cause question: an atypical fissure with systemic features.
**Off-midline** + diarrhoea + weight loss + low-grade fever + high calprotectin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Crohn's disease**.

elim: Haemorrhoids do not cause lateral fissures or weight loss.
Hard stool gives midline fissures, not diarrhoea.
IBS does not raise calprotectin or cause weight loss.
UC rarely causes perianal disease; Crohn's does.

steps.x: **A. Crohn's disease.**

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has bright red blood on the toilet paper after opening his bowels. He has been constipated. He wants to know whether it is a fissure or haemorrhoids.
practice.q: Which feature would most strongly suggest an anal fissure?
o: Prolapsing lump that reduces by itself
practice.e: Anal fissures are very painful on defecation; haemorrhoids typically cause painless bleeding, dripping, itch and prolapse.

steps.x: A distinguishing-feature question.

clues: bright red blood on the toilet paper
steps.x: Both conditions share fresh blood and constipation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Severe pain on defecation** points to fissure.

elim: Dripping blood is typical of haemorrhoids.
Itch is commoner with haemorrhoids.
Mucus suggests haemorrhoids or proctitis.
A prolapsing lump is a second-degree haemorrhoid.

steps.x: **E. Severe pain on defecation.**

practice.stem: A 63 year old man had a hip replacement 3 weeks ago. Since then he has had severe pain on defecation and bright red blood on the paper. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg. A posterior midline fissure is seen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely precipitating factor?
practice.e: Fissures are caused by hard stools and constipation; opioid analgesia after surgery is a classic cause.

steps.x: A cause question: what produced the hard stool.
Post-op, typical midline fissure. Medicines: **codeine and morphine**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Opioid-induced constipation**.

elim: Anticoagulants increase bleeding but do not tear the anoderm.
Positioning does not cause fissures.
Infection causes an abscess, not a midline tear.
A catheter has no link to fissures.

steps.x: **B. Opioid constipation.**

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has 10 days of pain on defecation and blood on the paper after a bout of constipation. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. A posterior midline fissure is seen. She has no weight loss or change in bowel habit.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: A typical posterior midline fissure with a clear cause and no red flags is a clinical diagnosis needing no investigation.

steps.x: Investigation for a typical fissure.

clues: no weight loss or change in bowel habit
steps.x: Typical site, clear cause, no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No investigation**: clinical diagnosis.

elim: Colonoscopy is for red flags or suspected IBD.
Calprotectin is for atypical fissures with bowel symptoms.
Sigmoidoscopy is not needed for a typical fissure.
MRI is for fistula or abscess anatomy.

steps.x: **E. No investigation.**

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has 2 months of anal pain and bleeding. He has lost 5 kg. Examination shows an indurated, irregular ulcer at the left lateral position of the anal margin, with a palpable inguinal lymph node.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
practice.e: An off-midline, indurated fissure with weight loss and a node in an older man suggests anal cancer: refer on the 2-week-wait pathway.

steps.x: Next step for a suspicious, atypical fissure.
Older, weight loss, **off-midline**, hard ulcer, node: malignancy until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent 2-week-wait** referral.

elim: FIT alone would delay assessment of a visible suspicious lesion.
Waiting delays a possible cancer diagnosis.
Treating as a simple fissure misses cancer.
Steroids are avoided and would delay diagnosis.

steps.x: **E. Two-week-wait referral.**

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has had 4 days of pain on defecation and bright red blood after hard stools. A posterior midline fissure is seen. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Dietary fibre, fluids, bulk laxative and analgesia
practice.e: An acute fissure is managed conservatively with fibre, fluids, a bulk-forming laxative such as ispaghula, simple analgesia and lubricant; steroids are avoided.

steps.x: Initial management of an acute fissure.
Acute (days), mechanical cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Conservative**: fibre, fluids, laxatives, analgesia.

elim: Botox is for refractory chronic fissures.
Surgery is for refractory chronic fissures.
Topical steroids should be avoided.
GTN is for chronic fissures.

steps.x: **B. Fibre, fluids, laxatives, analgesia.**

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has had a posterior midline anal fissure for 3 months despite a high-fibre diet, laxatives and topical lidocaine. There is a sentinel skin tag. Her BP is 120/78 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: A chronic fissure is first treated pharmacologically with topical 0.2% GTN for 6 to 8 weeks.

steps.x: Next step in a chronic fissure after conservative treatment.
**Chronic**, conservative treatment failed, no drug tried yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Topical 0.2% GTN** for 6–8 weeks.

elim: Botox comes after GTN and a calcium channel blocker fail.
Sphincterotomy is for refractory fissures.
Metronidazole is for perianal Crohn's or infection, not a typical fissure.
Steroids are avoided.

steps.x: **D. Topical 0.2% GTN.**

practice.stem: A 44 year old man with a chronic anal fissure started topical 0.2% GTN 10 days ago. He has stopped it because of severe headaches. His BP is 124/80 mmHg and pulse rate 72 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: If GTN is not tolerated, topical diltiazem (or oral nifedipine) is the next pharmacological option.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has a posterior midline anal fissure that has not healed after 3 months. Anorectal manometry shows a high resting pressure of the internal anal sphincter.
practice.q: Which is the most likely reason the fissure fails to heal?
o: Ischaemia from sphincter spasm in a watershed area

practice.e: The posterior midline is a watershed area with poor blood supply; internal sphincter spasm further reduces blood flow, creating a cycle of pain, spasm and poor healing.

steps.x: A pathophysiology question: why the fissure stays open.
Poor-supply site + high sphincter tone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ischaemia** from spasm in a **watershed** area.

elim: Bacteria are present but are not the main reason.
Mucus is not a factor.
Fissures are very painful; sensation is intact.
That describes haemorrhoids.

steps.x: **C. Ischaemia from spasm in a watershed area.**

glossary.anal fissure: A linear tear in the lining of the anal canal.
glossary.fissure in ano: Another name for an anal fissure.
glossary.anoderm: The thin, sensitive skin lining the lower anal canal.
glossary.anal verge: The outer edge of the anal canal where it meets perianal skin.
glossary.posterior midline: The back of the anal canal, in line with the natal cleft; the usual fissure site.
glossary.sentinel skin tag: A small tag of skin at the outer end of a chronic fissure.
glossary.sentinel pile: Another name for the sentinel skin tag of a chronic fissure.
glossary.internal anal sphincter: The involuntary smooth muscle ring of the anal canal; its spasm stops fissures healing.
glossary.watershed area: A region at the edge of two blood supplies with relatively poor perfusion.
glossary.haemorrhoids: Swollen anal vascular cushions; typically cause painless bright red bleeding.
glossary.thrombosed external haemorrhoid: A clotted haemorrhoid below the dentate line causing a tender purple lump.
glossary.perianal abscess: A pus collection near the anus causing constant throbbing pain and swelling.
glossary.fistula in ano: An abnormal track between the anal canal and perianal skin.
glossary.GTN: Glyceryl trinitrate, a nitric oxide donor that relaxes smooth muscle.
glossary.glyceryl trinitrate: A nitric oxide donor used as 0.2% ointment for chronic fissures.
glossary.nitric oxide: A signalling molecule that relaxes smooth muscle and widens blood vessels.
glossary.diltiazem: A calcium channel blocker used topically to relax the anal sphincter.
glossary.nifedipine: A calcium channel blocker that can be used orally or topically for fissures.
glossary.calcium channel blockers: Drugs that block calcium entry into smooth muscle, causing relaxation.
glossary.botulinum toxin: A nerve toxin injected to temporarily paralyse the internal anal sphincter.
glossary.lateral internal sphincterotomy: Surgery that divides part of the internal anal sphincter to reduce its tone.
glossary.ispaghula husk: A bulk-forming laxative (fibre supplement) that softens stools.
glossary.laxatives: Medicines that soften stool or help it pass.
glossary.osmotic: Drawing water into the bowel, as osmotic laxatives do.
glossary.faecal calprotectin: A stool test for bowel inflammation; raised in inflammatory bowel disease.
glossary.Crohn's disease: Inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gut, including the anus.
glossary.2-week-wait: The NHS urgent referral pathway for suspected cancer.
glossary.anal cancer: Usually squamous cell carcinoma of the anus; can mimic a fissure off the midline.
glossary.anorectal manometry: A test that measures pressures in the anal sphincters and rectum.
glossary.PR: Per rectum; a digital rectal examination.
glossary.co-codamol: Paracetamol combined with codeine; codeine causes constipation.
glossary.opioid: A morphine-like painkiller; constipation is a common side effect.
glossary.topical: Applied directly to the skin or affected area.
glossary.lidocaine: A local anaesthetic that can numb the anus before defecation.
